name: Epidermal growth factor (EGF)

lead: Epidermal growth factor (EGF) is a natural protein that tells skin cells to grow and repair. Serums with EGF are used by people who want smoother, younger-looking skin and softer wrinkles.

EGF binds receptors on skin cells, which drives cell turnover and repair. Its discoverers won a Nobel Prize, and a recombinant form is used medically for diabetic foot ulcers. For facial skin aging, one small serum trial has been registered, with no published results.

paras: People use EGF as a cosmetic serum applied to the face, usually in a regular morning or evening routine alongside moisturiser and sunscreen. It is often grouped with other growth-factor and peptide skincare ingredients. Skin-texture changes from this kind of product are typically judged over weeks of consistent use.

Safety of medical EGF is described as poorly studied, and EGF signalling is a research focus in cancer biology. No study found has tested cosmetic EGF for cancer risk. Serums vary in formulation and as cosmetics are not held to drug-style approval.

angle.text: EGF serums aim at smoother, younger-looking skin: the protein binds skin cell receptors, which increases cell turnover and repair. The biology of EGF is well described, and one small serum trial for skin aging has been registered.

lead: Epidermal growth factor (EGF) is a small protein of 53 amino acids that stimulates cell growth, differentiation and survival by binding the EGF receptor (EGFR) on cell surfaces.[1] It was the second growth factor to be identified; Stanley Cohen found it while working with Rita Levi-Montalcini, and the two shared the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.[1][2]

In cosmetics, recombinant or synthetic EGF appears as an ingredient in serums and in clinic treatments, where marketing describes it as supporting skin renewal and repair. People using these products are aiming for smoother, more even, better-hydrated skin and softer fine lines. The chain they describe is that EGF signals skin cells to divide and renew, which proponents say can improve texture over weeks. In looksmaxxing and skincare discussion it is grouped with other growth-factor and peptide ingredients, and is often paired with microneedling or similar procedures.[3]

Medically, a recombinant human EGF product (Heberprot-P) is used for diabetic foot ulcers, with evidence of improved healing described as tentative and safety as poorly studied.[1][4] For skin appearance, a 2023 systematic review of topical growth-factor preparations (of which EGF products are one group) reported modest investigator-rated improvements in texture and fine lines across 33 mostly small studies, and one registered trial has examined an EGF facial serum specifically.[5][6]
infobox: 53 amino acids, about 6 kDa; three disulfide bridges [1]
Stanley Cohen with Rita Levi-Montalcini; Nobel Prize 1986 [1][2]
Platelets, urine, saliva, milk, tears, plasma [1]
Ingredient in some serums; plant-derived (barley) and recombinant forms are sold [8]

paras: EGF binds EGFR with high affinity and induces receptor dimerization, activating the receptor's tyrosine kinase and starting a signaling cascade that raises intracellular calcium, increases glycolysis and protein synthesis, and ultimately drives DNA synthesis and cell proliferation.[1] It occurs in platelets, urine, saliva, milk, tears and plasma and is produced in the submandibular and parotid glands.[1] Salivary EGF is reported to help maintain the integrity of oral, esophageal and gastric tissue, including healing of ulcers and protection of the mucosa from acid, bile acids and enzymes.[1]

The human molecule has three disulfide bridges (Cys6-Cys20, Cys14-Cys31, Cys33-Cys42) that form the loops needed for high-affinity receptor binding.[1] EGF is the founding member of a protein family that includes HB-EGF, TGF-alpha, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin and neuregulins 1 to 4, all sharing a conserved cysteine-rich motif.[1] A 1990 review in the Journal of Biological Chemistry summarised its structure and receptor biology.[7]
Human EGF has several names in the literature, including epithelial growth factor and urogastrone, the name originally given to the human form because of its effect on gastric acid secretion.[1]

Stanley Cohen was born in Brooklyn in 1922, trained in chemistry, zoology and biochemistry, and moved to Washington University in St. Louis in 1952.[2] There he worked with Rita Levi-Montalcini on nerve growth factor. During that work he isolated a protein that accelerated incisor eruption and eyelid opening in newborn mice; it was later named epidermal growth factor.[1][2]

Early work also described a secreted peptide in mouse submaxillary glands and in human urine, and the human form was originally called urogastrone.[1] Cohen moved to Vanderbilt University School of Medicine in 1959 and retired in 1999.[2]

Cohen and Levi-Montalcini received the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries of growth factors, EGF among them.[1][2] Cohen also received the Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research and the US National Medal of Science in 1986, and died in 2020.[2]

subs.h: From laboratory protein to skincare ingredient
paras: Because EGF drives the proliferation of epithelial cells and has a role in wound repair, it became a candidate for wound-healing products and, later, for cosmetic use. Recombinant EGF is now used as a cosmetic ingredient. One widely discussed skincare serum from an Icelandic company lists EGF produced in transgenic barley, and the company has said its EGF is not human-derived.[8] A skincare writer reviewing that product in 2016 described it as a quick boost she did not use long-term, and noted that the question of safety circulates among skincare enthusiasts.[8]

Growth-factor ingredients have reached mainstream skincare coverage; a HuffPost article updated in 2023 describes growth factors as a youth-boosting skincare trend and quotes dermatologists on the claims.[3]

Recombinant human EGF sold as Heberprot-P can be injected into or applied to diabetic foot ulcers. Wikipedia reports tentative evidence of improved healing and, citing a 2015 Cochrane review, says safety has been poorly studied.[1] The Cochrane review analysed a heterogeneous group of trials assessing 11 growth factors for diabetic foot ulcers and noted that safety data were poorly reported and that adverse events may have been underestimated.[4]

EGF is also used in laboratory work on bioengineered grafts, where synthetic scaffolds are modified with it, and in bone-regeneration research, where EGF at low nanogram concentrations promoted osteogenic differentiation of dental pulp stem cells in culture.[1]

EGF appears in serums, often alongside other peptides and growth factors, and in clinic-applied treatments that combine EGF-containing solutions with microneedling, microinfusion or similar methods meant to help the protein reach the skin. Proponents say topical EGF promotes skin renewal, hydration and fine-line reduction, drawing on its role in wound repair.[3] The target outcomes are skin texture, evenness, hydration and softer fine lines, usually discussed over weeks to months of regular use.

EGF is a protein of about 6 kDa.[1] Skincare discussion often raises whether a protein of this size reaches deeper skin layers from a simple serum, which is why delivery-assisting procedures such as microneedling are discussed alongside the ingredient; the topic has not been settled by the studies reviewed here.[3]

Dermatologists quoted in a 2023 HuffPost feature describe growth factors as signalling proteins that can reduce fine lines and improve texture. One calls the effects on collagen, elasticity and wrinkles good but still modest, and notes that no standardized protocols or guidelines exist for topical growth factors.[3] Another says there are no studies supporting the hypothesis that growth factors cause skin cancer, while a third notes controversy in the dermatology community about excess cell growth and cautions that the FDA mostly regulates skincare as cosmetics, so the term can be used without prior approval.[3]

Because EGF signals through a pathway that promotes cell proliferation, researchers study the EGF pathway in cancer. Laboratory work has linked EGF to melanoma lymph node metastasis in a mouse model,[9] and an EGF gene variant (A61G) has been associated with esophageal adenocarcinoma risk.[10] These studies concern the biology of the pathway and not topical cosmetic products, and no study found has tested cancer risk from cosmetic EGF.
Drugs that block EGFR are an established class of cancer treatment, which is the setting for most clinical research that mentions EGF or its receptor.[11]

Brands and commentators take different positions. A manufacturer quoted by a skincare writer argues that EGF will not turn normal cells into cancer cells, while the same writer suggests that people with a melanoma history use their own judgment and regards human-derived EGF as best avoided.[8]

A 2023 systematic review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology covered prospective studies from 2000 to October 2022 of topical growth-factor preparations for facial rejuvenation. It included 33 studies (9 randomized controlled trials and 24 uncontrolled case series) with 1,180 participants using 23 different preparations. Investigators reported modest improvements in skin texture, fine lines and wrinkles and overall appearance versus baseline, participants rated their improvement higher than investigators did, and adverse events were low-risk. The authors noted large variation in growth-factor sources and outcome measures and that durability beyond 6 months is unknown. This review spans all growth factors, not EGF alone.[6]

A registered trial (NCT05724589) evaluated an EGF serum for facial skin hydration, elasticity, pigmentation and wrinkles in 28 participants, started in January 2023 and listed as completed; no results were available in the registry entry reviewed.[5] Larger trials of the EGFR-blocking antibody panitumumab (ABX-EGF) were cancer treatment studies and do not concern cosmetic EGF.[11]

lore.intro: EGF is discussed mainly as a skincare serum ingredient alongside peptides and growth factors in skincare communities and media; little looksmaxxing forum material specific to EGF exists to document.
